questions.question:
(i) (a) When does the nucleus of an atom tend to become radioactive?
(b) Name a single pulley in which displacement of load and effort is not the same.
(c) State one advantage of this pulley.
questions.solution:
(a) When the number of neutrons becomes much greater than the number of protons (n/p > 1 by a large margin), the nucleus tends to become radioactive.
(b) Single movable pulley (displacement of effort = 2 x displacement of load).
(c) Its mechanical advantage is 2, i.e. the load can be lifted by applying an effort equal to half the load.

marking_points.point: n/p ratio much greater than 1 (neutrons far exceed protons) makes nucleus radioactive
Advantage: mechanical advantage 2 / effort is half the load

questions.topic: Centre of gravity of triangular lamina
concepts: moment of weight about suspension point
questions.question:
(ii) (a) What is the position of centre of gravity of a triangular lamina?
(b) When this triangular lamina is suspended freely from any one vertex, what is the moment of force produced by its own weight in its rest position?
questions.solution:
(a) At the centroid, the point of intersection of the medians.
(b) Zero: the line of action of the weight passes through the axis of rotation (algebraic sum of moments is zero).

marking_points.point: Centre of gravity at centroid / intersection of medians
Moment is zero (line of action of weight passes through the point of suspension)

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.question:
(iii) The diagram shows wheel O pivoted at point A. Three equal forces F1, F2 and F3 act at point B on the wheel.
(a) Which force will produce maximum moment about A?
(b) Give a reason for your answer in (a).
questions.solution:
(a) Force F1.
(b) The perpendicular distance of F1 from A (AQ) is the maximum: AQ > AR > AP, so F1 has the greatest moment.

marking_points.point: Reason: perpendicular distance of F1 from pivot A is greatest

questions.figure_desc: A wheel with centre O pivoted at point A on its rim; three equal forces F1, F2, F3 act at point B in different directions; perpendiculars from A to their lines of action are AQ (for F1), AR (for F2), AP (for F3), with AQ > AR > AP.

questions.question:
(iv) (a) What should be the angle between the direction of force and the direction of displacement, for work to be negative?
(b) Name the physical quantity obtained using the formula U/h, where U is the potential energy and h is the height.
questions.solution:
(a) 180° (W = Fs cos 180° = -Fs, negative).
(b) Weight (U/h = mgh/h = mg, the weight of the body).

questions.question: (v) Calculate the power spent by a crane while lifting a load of mass 2000 kg, at velocity of 1.5 ms⁻¹. (g = 10 ms⁻²)
questions.solution: Power = force x velocity = mg x v = 2000 x 10 x 1.5 = 30000 W.

marking_points.point: Formula P = F x v = mgv

questions.question:
(vi) A metal foot ruler is held at the edge of a table. It is pressed at its free end and then released. It vibrates.
(a) Name the vibrations produced.
(b) State one way to increase the frequency of these vibrations.
questions.solution:
(a) Damped vibrations (the amplitude decreases with time); free (natural) vibrations is also acceptable.
(b) Reduce the length of the vibrating part of the ruler to increase the frequency.
Note: the board key says 'damped vibrations'.

marking_points.point: Reduce the free length of the ruler

concepts: power and voltage rating of appliance
questions.question: (vii) 'A geyser is rated 240 W - 220 V'. Explain the meaning of this statement.
questions.solution: When the geyser is connected to a 220 V supply, it consumes 240 J of electrical energy per second (power 240 W).

marking_points.point: Consumes 240 J of energy every second (power 240 W)

concepts: focal length unaffected by covering part of lens
questions.question:
(i) (a) Is it possible for a concave lens to form an image of size two times that of the object? Write Yes or No.
(b) What will happen to the focal length of the lens if a part of the lens is covered with an opaque paper?
questions.solution:
(a) No. A concave lens always forms a virtual, diminished image.
(b) No change in focal length, since the refractive index and radii of curvature do not change; only the intensity (brightness) of the image changes.

marking_points.point: Focal length unchanged (only intensity of image decreases)

concepts: fuse or MCB in live wire
questions.question:
(ii) (a) Which electrical component protects the electric circuit in case of excess current and which can also be used as a switch?
(b) Name the wire to which this electrical component is connected in an electric circuit.

answer_items.prompt: Electrical component that protects the circuit from excess current and can be used as a switch
Wire to which it is connected

questions.solution: (a) Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB). It trips and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value, and it can also be switched on and off by hand. (A fuse protects but cannot be used as a switch.) (b) Live wire.

questions.question:
(iv) Thermal capacities of substances A and B are same. If mass of A is more than mass of B then:
(a) Which substance will have more specific heat capacity?
(b) Which substance will show greater rise in temperature if the same amount of heat is supplied to both?
questions.solution:
(a) Substance B: specific heat capacity = thermal capacity / mass, so smaller mass means greater specific heat capacity.
(b) Since thermal capacities are the same, both A and B show the same rise in temperature.

marking_points.point: B has more specific heat capacity (c = thermal capacity/mass)
Both show the same rise in temperature (equal thermal capacities)

questions.question: (v) How is the radioactivity of a radio isotope affected if it undergoes a chemical change? Give a reason for your answer.
questions.solution: There is no change. Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon and is not affected by chemical change, which involves only the electrons.

marking_points.point: Reason: radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon; chemical changes involve only electrons

concepts: prism deviation formula d = i1 + i2 - A
questions.question:
(i) The diagram below shows the ray OP travelling through an equilateral prism of a certain material. The angle of incidence i1 at P is 65°.
(a) Calculate the value of i2, if the angle of deviation is 43°.
(b) What is the ray QS called?
questions.solution:
(a) Deviation d = i1 + i2 - A, so 43 = 65 + i2 - 60, giving i2 = 38 degrees.
(b) QS is the emergent ray.

concepts: total internal reflection at critical angle in prism
questions.question: (ii) Copy the diagram given below and complete the path of the light ray PQ, as it emerges out of the prism by marking necessary angles. The critical angle of glass is 42°.
questions.solution: The ray PQ is incident normally on face AB, so it enters undeviated at Q. It meets the base BC at an angle of incidence of 60°, which is more than the critical angle 42°, so it is totally internally reflected at BC (angle of reflection 60°). The reflected ray strikes face AC normally (angle of incidence 0°) and emerges undeviated, perpendicular to AC. Mark the 60° angles of incidence and reflection at BC and the 90° at AC.

marking_points.point: Ray enters AB undeviated and is totally internally reflected at base BC since angle of incidence 60° > critical angle 42°
Reflected ray drawn with angle of reflection 60° towards face AC
Ray emerges from AC along the normal (undeviated), angles marked

questions.figure_desc: An equilateral glass prism ABC with ray PQ inside striking face at Q; angles of 60° and 90° are marked; critical angle of glass is 42°.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Refraction of coloured rays in glass
questions.question:
(iii) The diagram below shows two parallel rays A (Orange) & B (Blue) incident from air, on air-glass boundary.
(a) Copy and complete the path of the rays A and B.
(b) How do the speeds of these rays differ in glass?
(c) Are the two refracted rays in glass parallel? Give a reason.
questions.solution:
(a) Both rays bend towards the normal in glass; the blue ray deviates more (bends more) than the orange ray.
(b) The speed of blue is less than that of orange because the wavelength of blue is less than that of orange.
(c) No, the refracted rays are not parallel because of different wavelengths (different refractive indices) of the two colours.

marking_points.point: Both rays refract towards the normal, blue deviating more than orange
Blue travels slower than orange in glass
Not parallel, with reason (different wavelengths/refractive index)

questions.figure_desc: Two parallel rays, A (orange) and B (blue), incident from air on a plane air-glass boundary.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question: (i) A convex lens of focal length 10 cm is placed at a distance of 60 cm from a screen. How far from the lens should an object be placed so as to obtain a real image on the screen?
questions.solution: Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with v = 60 cm, f = 10 cm: 1/60 - 1/u = 1/10, so 1/u = 1/60 - 1/10 = -1/12, u = -12 cm. The object should be placed 12 cm in front of the lens.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(ii) (a) A coin kept inside water (refractive index 4/3) when viewed from air in a vertical direction appears to be raised by 3.0 mm. Find the depth of the coin in water.
(b) How is the critical angle related to the refractive index of a medium?
questions.solution:
(a) mu = real depth / apparent depth, so mu - 1 = (real - apparent)/apparent = 3 mm / apparent depth. 1/3 = 3/apparent, apparent depth = 9 mm; real depth = 9 + 3 = 12 mm.
(b) mu = 1 / sin(critical angle).

marking_points.point: Use mu = real depth/apparent depth (shift = real - apparent)
Apparent depth 9 mm and real depth 12 mm

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(iii) (a) Infrared radiations are used in warfare. Explain with reason, why.
(b) A ray of light is incident at 45° on an equilateral prism in the diagram (the ray splits into red and violet on emerging).
1. Name the phenomenon exhibited by the ray of light when it enters and emerges out of the prism.
2. State the cause of the above phenomenon mentioned by you.
questions.solution:
(a) Every warm body (soldiers, vehicles, weapons) emits infrared radiation. Infrared detectors / night-vision devices pick up this radiation, so enemy targets can be seen and tracked in darkness, fog or haze (infrared is also scattered less). Hence infrared is used in warfare.
(b) 1. Dispersion of light (the white light is refracted and split into its constituent colours, red deviating least and violet most).
2. Cause: light of different colours travels with different speeds in glass, so the refractive index of glass is different for different colours (wavelengths) and each colour is deviated by a different amount.

marking_points.point: (a) Infrared used for night vision / detecting enemy targets in darkness or fog
(a) Reason: warm bodies emit infrared which IR detectors can sense
(b)2 Different colours have different speeds / refractive index in glass

questions.figure_desc: An equilateral prism with a ray incident at 45° on one face; on the other side the emergent light is spread into a spectrum with red at the top (least deviated) and violet at the bottom (most deviated).

concepts: centre of gravity of metre scale
questions.question:
(ii) A metre scale of weight 50 gf can be balanced at 40 cm mark without any weight suspended on it.
(a) If this ruler is cut at its centre then state which part [0 to 50 cm or 50 to 100 cm] of the ruler will weigh more than 25 gf.
(b) What minimum weight placed on this metre ruler can balance this ruler when it is pivoted at its centre?
questions.solution:
(a) The 0 to 50 cm part weighs more, because the balance point (centre of gravity) is at 40 cm, nearer that end.
(b) Pivoted at 50 cm: 50 x 10 = x x 50, so x = 10 gf (printed key: 10 gf).

marking_points.point: Reason: centre of gravity at 40 cm, closer to the 0-50 cm side

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Work and power of car engine
questions.question:
(iii) A car of mass 120 kg is moving at a speed 18 km/h and it accelerates to attain a speed of 54 km/h in 5 seconds. Calculate:
(a) the work done by the engine.
(b) the power of the engine.
questions.solution:
u = 18 km/h = 5 m/s; v = 54 km/h = 15 m/s.
(a) Work done = change in KE = 1/2 x 120 x (15^2 - 5^2) = 12000 J.
(b) Power = work/time = 12000/5 = 2400 W.

marking_points.point: Conversion of speeds to 5 m/s and 15 m/s

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(i) (a) Which characteristic of sound is affected due to the larger surface of a school bell?
(b) Calculate the distance covered by the Ultrasonic wave having a velocity of 1.5 km s⁻¹ in 14 s, when it is received after reflection by the receiver of the SONAR.
questions.solution:
(a) Loudness (amplitude).
(b) Total distance covered by the wave = v × t = 1.5 km s⁻¹ × 14 s = 21 km; since the wave travels to the obstacle and back, the distance of the obstacle from the SONAR = 21/2 = 10.5 km.

marking_points.point: Formula d = v x t (or d = vt/2 for the distance of the reflecting object) with substitution
21 km total path covered by the wave (accept 10.5 km if stated as the distance of the obstacle)

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(iii) We are able to see the T.V. channels clearly when we set T.V. on auto-tuning.
(a) Which phenomenon led to the clear visibility of the channels, due to auto-tuning?
(b) Define the above phenomenon mentioned by you.
(c) Give any one more example of this phenomenon.
questions.solution:
(a) Resonance.
(b) Resonance: the phenomenon in which a body vibrates with increased amplitude under the influence of an external periodic force whose frequency is exactly equal to the natural frequency of the body.
(c) The air in the sound box of a musical instrument vibrates with larger amplitude due to the vibrating string.

marking_points.point: Definition: frequency of external periodic force equals natural frequency, giving large amplitude
One valid example (e.g. sound box of a musical instrument)

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(i) (a) Define specific resistance.
(b) What happens to the specific resistance of a conductor if its length is doubled?
(c) Name a substance whose specific resistance remains almost unchanged with the increase in its temperature.
questions.solution:
(a) Specific resistance (resistivity) is the resistance offered by a conductor of unit length and unit cross-section: rho = RA/l.
(b) It does not change; it depends only on the material and temperature.
(c) Constantan, manganin, etc.

marking_points.point: Definition: resistance of conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(ii) (a) Which nuclear radiation will travel undeviated in an electric field?
(b) How can one stop the radiations escaping from a nuclear reactor in a nuclear power plant?
(c) Name one internal source of background radiations.
questions.solution:
(a) Gamma radiation (photons with no charge).
(b) Shield the reactor with thick steel/lead walls (and concrete).
(c) Radioactive potassium-40 (or carbon-14) present inside the human body.

marking_points.point: Internal source: radioactive K-40 or C-14 present inside the human body

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(iii) Find the value of current I drawn from the cell. The circuit has a cell of e.m.f. 3.4 V and internal resistance 2 ohm, with two 15 ohm resistors in series, and this combination is in parallel with a 30 ohm resistor.
(a) Calculate the current I.
(b) Calculate the terminal voltage.
questions.solution:
(a) The two 15 ohm resistors in series give 30 ohm; this is in parallel with 30 ohm, giving 15 ohm. I = E/(R + r) = 3.4/(15 + 2) = 0.2 A.
(b) Terminal voltage = E - Ir = 3.4 - 0.2 x 2 = 3 V.

marking_points.point: Parallel with 30 ohm gives 15 ohm; I = E/(R+r) = 0.2 A

questions.figure_desc: Circuit: cell 3.4 V with internal resistance 2 ohm; two 15 ohm resistors in series, that branch in parallel with a 30 ohm resistor; current I drawn from the cell.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question: (i) Calculate the total amount of heat energy required to melt 200 g of ice at 0°C to water at 100°C. (Specific latent heat of ice = 336 J g⁻¹, specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
questions.solution: Heat to melt ice = 200 x 336 = 67200 J. Heat to warm water 0 to 100 C = 200 x 4.2 x 100 = 84000 J. Total = 67200 + 84000 = 151200 J.

marking_points.point: Heat for raising temperature = mc(dT) = 84000 J

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(ii) (a) State the principle of calorimetry.
(b) Name the material used for making a calorimeter.
(c) Write one characteristic property of the material chosen for making a calorimeter.
questions.solution:
(a) When two or more bodies at different temperatures are brought in contact, heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body, provided there is no heat loss to the surroundings.
(b) Copper.
(c) It should have a low specific heat capacity (good conductor of heat).

marking_points.point: Heat lost by hot body = heat gained by cold body (no loss to surroundings)
Low specific heat capacity / good conductor

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
(iii) The diagram shows a cardboard on which iron filings are kept. A wire bent in the form of a loop passes through the cardboard. When current flows through it the iron filings arrange themselves as shown.
(a) State the polarities of the battery at A and B.
(b) State the effect on the magnetic field if an iron rod is held along the axis of the coil.
(c) State one way to: 1. Change the polarity of the coil. 2. Decrease the strength of the magnetic field around the coil.
questions.solution:
(a) A is positive and B is negative (field lines anticlockwise on the left side of the loop, so current goes upward there).
(b) The magnetic field strength increases.
(c) 1. Reverse the direction of the current. 2. Decrease the current (strength of current).
questions.figure_desc: A cardboard with iron filings arranged in concentric circles around a wire loop passing through it; battery terminals A and B connected to the loop.
